title: Target slice and direct algebraic bounds

add.label: Direct ledger
add.name: Generic bound
add.statement: Under (P5), E(2Q+2) ≤ (Q+1)/2^λ for every integer 0 ≤ Q < 2^λ.
add.proof: The coefficient of u² in E is (θ+ε_f)/2+9ε_f/2 ≥ 0, so E is convex. By (P5) its values at 2 and 2^{λ+1} are at most 2^{-λ} and 1, respectively. The affine function u/2^{λ+1} has exactly these endpoint values, so it bounds E from above on the interval by convexity. Set u=2Q+2.
add.explain: Direct derivation from the linked premises.

add.label: Direct gp-rank
add.name: Rank bound
add.statement: For either sampler and every stack W of rank d, gp(W)≤g^{−d}. For every v in its row space, gp(vᵀ)≥gp(W).
add.proof: Stack the rows as M. If its column 0 is nonzero, include that column in a column basis; otherwise omit it. Once the coordinates outside that basis are fixed, the equation Mr=u determines the pivot coordinates uniquely modulo q. If 0 is outside the basis, it need not be conditioned on, since it has zero column. The positive-index pivots each hit their prescribed values with independent probability 1/g or zero, and if 0 is a pivot its conditional probability given all positive indices is at most 1/g. Thus each fiber has probability ≤g^{−d}. Since vᵀr is a linear image of Mr, the largest fiber of Mr maps to one value of vᵀr, giving the other inequality.
add.explain: Direct derivation from the linked premises.

add.label: Direct qap
add.name: QAP criterion
add.statement:
For any admissible evaluation points and symmetric W, passage is equivalent to each of the identities
P_W−W_{00} L_ρ=h Z(X−ρ)+Z_0 R,
P_W=h′ Z+Z_0 R,
when the remainder R is allowed. In either identity the remainder is R_W, the interpolant of degree below ν n_c of P_W/Z_0 on the cosets; the quotients have deg h<D−1 and deg h′<D. For a witness these identities apply to wwᵀ with W_{00}=1.
add.proof: For either identity, evaluation on the cosets forces R=R_W because Z vanishes there and Z_0 does not. The sums of its values there are the constraint tests by the QAP table. For exponents divisible by ν, the matrix of coset sums is ν times the Vandermonde matrix on the distinct νth powers of the coset representatives; the other exponents give zero. With no cosets the allowed remainder is zero and there are no constraint tests. Otherwise invertibility makes the constraint tests equivalent to R_W being allowed. Subtract Z_0 R_W from P_W. On the roots of Z the difference vanishes except possibly at d_j for 1≤j≤N, where its values are the Booleanity tests. Subtracting W_{00}L_ρ adds the root ρ without changing those values. Hence divisibility by the respective vanishing polynomials is equivalent to the remaining tests. The numerators have degree ≤2D−2 since Z_0 R_W and L_ρ have degree ≤D−1, so division by polynomials of degrees D and D−1 yields the claimed bounds. A witness passes the tests by its defining equations.
add.explain: Direct derivation from the linked premises.

add.label: Direct classification
add.name: Classification
add.statement: A nonzero usable stack with row space of dimension at most three and no kernel vector has a witness in its row space.
add.proof:
Work over K=F_{q^n}. Let U have an F_q-basis of the row space as columns, d its column count, u_j the transpose of its row j, and h_s=Uᵀσ^s(z). No kernel vector means the entries of h_0 are F_q-independent. For s=a,b,c with a=n/2−1,b=n/2,c=n/2+1, assemble W_s from the U-weight coefficients, V-weight coefficients, and the σ^c conjugate of the U assembly, respectively. These have a unique expression W_s=UM_sUᵀ with M_s symmetric: applying a left inverse of U on both sides gives M_s, and the row and column spaces ensure the reconstruction. The ties imply M_s h_t=M_t h_s. The first d of these h_s are independent: a relation with coefficients λ_j would give the nonzero q-linear polynomial Σ_{j<d} λ_j X^{q^j} vanishing on all entries of h_a, hence on their F_q-span of q^d elements. Frobenius preserves their independence and the polynomial has degree at most q^{d−1}, a contradiction. Thus the h_s span K^d. Thus h_s↦M_s extends linearly, since any relation Σ_s λ_s h_s=0 gives (Σ_s λ_s M_s)h_t=0 for every t. Its trilinear form T(h,u,v)=uᵀM(h)v is symmetric by matrix symmetry and the ties on spanning arguments. The tests give T(h,u_j,u_j−u_0)=0 for every h, by linearity from h_s. Writing M_s for M(h_s), we have M_a=σ^a(M_c) and M_b=σ^b(M_b) by the conjugacy and even-degree V assembly.
If u_0=0, choose d of the u_j as a basis. T vanishes on basis triples with repetitions, so can be nonzero only for d=3, with one independent value t on the triples of distinct indices. In those basis coordinates the off-diagonal evaluations of M_s are t times the three coordinates of h_s. The two conjugacy identities, using σ^a(h_c)=σ^b(h_b)=h_0 and the basis over F_q, imply t h_a=σ^a(t)h_0 and t h_b=σ^b(t)h_0. The spanning condition for three vectors in dimension three rules out both h_a,h_b proportional to h_0. Thus t=0, and T=0 would make the stack zero.
With u_0≠0, complete it to a basis u_0,l_1,…,l_{d−1} from the rows. For each binary tuple δ of length d−1 let p_δ be the dual-coordinate vector taking values 1,δ_1,…,δ_{d−1} on this basis, and write w_δ=Up_δ and z_δ=z(w_δ)≠0. The test relations replace each repeated nonzero index of a basis triple by index 0 until distinct; symmetry then makes each triple's value depend only on its set A of nonzero indices. The cubes (hᵀp_δ)(uᵀp_δ)(vᵀp_δ) have entries ∏_{j∈A}δ_j on these triples. The matrix of these entries, indexing tuples by their support B, is the subset incidence matrix 1_{A⊆B}, triangular with unit diagonal under cardinality order. Hence T is a linear combination of these cubes with coefficients c_δ∈K. Pairs also realize all subsets A since d−1≤2; the same matrix proves independence of the squares p_δp_δᵀ.
It follows that M_s=Σ_δ c_δ σ^s(z_δ)p_δp_δᵀ. Comparing square coefficients in the two conjugacy identities shows c_δ/z_δ fixed by σ^a and σ^b, hence by σ since b−a=1. Write χ_δ=c_δ/z_δ∈F_q. Now take any linear passage test L over F_q. It vanishes on every W_s by vanishing on the stack coefficients. Consequently h_0ᵀQh_s=0, where Q=Σ_δ χ_δ L(w_δw_δᵀ)p_δp_δᵀ is over F_q. Spanning gives h_0ᵀQ=0, and F_q-independence of the entries of h_0 gives Q=0. Independence of the squares gives χ_δ L(w_δw_δᵀ)=0 for each δ. Some χ_δ is nonzero, since otherwise all assemblies and thus the stack vanish. The corresponding w_δ has coordinate 0 equal to 1 and its moment matrix passes every test, hence it is a witness.

add.label: Direct half
add.name: Factor one half
add.statement: In the experiment of Definition 3.6, $\Pr[\, b' = b \wedge \mathsf{Fail} \,] \le \frac12 + \frac14 (f_0 + f_1)$.
add.proof: Fix the shared coins in the uniform-masked-message game. By the coupling, either both bits lead to a target query or neither does; off the target event the same output guesses at most one bit correctly. Hence, putting p=Pr[Tgt], the off-target contribution to success with failure is at most (1−p)/2. On target it is at most f=(f_0+f_1)/2≤p, the probability of target with failure. Their sum is ≤1/2+f/2.

add.label: Direct inverse
add.name: Inverse theorem
add.statement: Under (I1)–(I6) in the linked inverse conditions, every nonzero v∈F_q^{N+1} with v_0=0 and gp(vᵀ)>θ has a short multiple x with x_0=0.
add.proof:
Use the full inverse conditions throughout. Write ε=ε_tr and μ=μ_tr. Work with the box of independently uniform coordinates in {2,…,g+1} and use the notation of lattice height, density and trimming. For a rank-e lattice, choosing e independent rows of its basis determines their box coordinates uniquely from the target fiber and the remaining coordinates. Each such integer tuple has conditional probability at most g^{−e}.

Trimming loss. For a lattice Θ of rank d∈{1,2,3} with basis B, a centered uniform box coordinate X has moment generating function sinh(gt/2)/(g sinh(t/2)) by the finite geometric sum (with value 1 at zero). It is bounded by sinh(gt/2)/(gt/2)≤exp(g²t²/24): the first inequality is sinh(u)/u≥1 for real u, and the second follows termwise from (2j+1)!≥6^j j!. Therefore the centered projected vector Y=Bᵀr_I−y_Θ satisfies E exp(uᵀY)≤exp(uᵀΣ_Θu/2) by independence. Set Z=Σ_Θ^{−1/2}Y and let G be an independent standard normal of dimension d. Integrating first in G gives E exp(99‖Z‖²/200)=E exp(√(99/100)GᵀZ). Integrating first in Z bounds this by E exp(99‖G‖²/200)=10^d. Markov's inequality at R_tr² gives deleted mass at most 10^d exp(−99R_tr²/200)≤ε by (I2) for d≤3.

Coordinate and lift facts. If B is a basis matrix and J rows of a largest minor, Cramer's rule bounds the coefficients of B_i B_J^{-1} by 1 in magnitude: they are ratios of maximal minors, or zero. Thus restriction onto J is injective on the span and bounds every coordinate by the ℓ₁ norm there. For a saturated lattice, extending B to a unimodular matrix gives an integral left inverse from the first rows of the inverse matrix. Transposing makes Bᵀ onto the integer codomain. For an integral matrix Δ of rank k with all k-minors below q in magnitude, use Smith normal form UΔV=S. Its nonzero k-minor survives mod q, so all k nonzero diagonal entries of S are units mod q. If cᵀΔ≡0, the first k entries of cᵀU^{-1} are multiples of q. Zero those entries and multiply by U; the result is an integral relation with residue cᵀ.

Prefix bounds. Take a saturated rank-d lattice Θ and put a largest minor J first in the coordinate order. For d≤k≤|I| let Θ_k be the lattice of integer points in the real span of the restricted basis columns, with height h_k and density m_k.
For a basis B of Θ, denote its first k rows by B_k and write B_k=Y_k C_k with Y_k a saturated prefix basis and C_k an integral nonsingular matrix. The transpose image G_k=B_kᵀ Z^k has index |det C_k| by surjectivity of Y_kᵀ. Each maximal minor scales by |det C_k|, so J remains maximal and h_k[Z^d:G_k]=h(Θ). The first prefix has full span and saturation Z^d, with height 1 and point fibers of mass g^{−d}; the last lattice is Θ. Adding the next row enlarges G_k by its cyclic class of order s_k, so its order equals h_{k+1}/h_k. In a fiber of B_{k+1}ᵀ the new coordinate is in at most one residue class modulo s_k, since the old contribution lies in G_k. Since C_kᵀ is injective, the old fiber definitions agree, giving conditional density ≤m_k for each of the at most ⌈g/s_k⌉ choices. Hence m_{k+1}≤m_k⌈g/s_k⌉/g, and s_k≥g forces a single new-coordinate value.
For a step with s=s_k<g, we show m_{k+1}^b h_{k+1}^{b−1}≤m_k^b h_k^{b−1}. For s=1 this follows from the density bound. For 2≤s<g it suffices that 1+s/g≤s^{1/b}, since ⌈g/s⌉/g≤(1+s/g)/s. For s≥2^b the left side is ≤2≤s^{1/b}. For 2≤s≤2^b it suffices to replace g by 2^b and use concavity of s^{1/b}−1−s/2^b, zero at 2^b and positive at 2 by (ln 2)/b>2^{1−b} for b≥7 (true at 7 and b/2^{b−1} decreases). Thus m_{k+1}≤m_k s^{−1+1/b}; raising to b and multiplying by h_{k+1}^{b−1} proves the product bound.
For d=3, put h=h(Θ), and multiply the density factors for the r steps with s_k>1, whose product of height ratios is h. The upper product ∏(1/s_k+1/g) exceeds ∏1/s_k=1/h by at most r(1/2+1/g)^{r−1}/g: telescope over the r factor replacements, bounding all other factors by 1/2+1/g. For r=0 there is zero increase. For r≥1 the bound is at most (1+2/g)/g, since the numerator decreases after r=2 by the consecutive ratio (1+1/r)(1/2+1/g)<1 for r≥2. Thus m(Θ)≤g^{−3}(1/h+ξ_tr/g)≤g^{−3}ξ_tr(1/h+1/g). With m(Θ)≥μ_tr this gives h≤H_3 by (I2), and m(Θ)h≤g^{−3}ξ_tr(1+H_3/g)≤Γ_3/g³ by (I4).

Sparse images. A nonempty box set F on I and one additional coordinate is trimmed by a lattice Θ on I of rank d∈{1,2,3}, with |I|≤N. Use Φ(r)=(Bᵀr_I,r_{i′}). In case (a), the image has affine dimension d+1 and lies in an index-q coset. We will bound Pr[F] by Λ_d g^d h(Θ)m(Θ)/q. In case (b), the normal lattice F^⊥ has rank d′ between 1 and d−1, a largest minor at J⊆I, and its restrictions to I lie in the span of Θ. We will bound Pr[F]h(F^⊥) by Λ_{d−d′}g^{d−d′}h(Θ)m(Θ).
Every image point of Φ carries box mass at most m(Θ)/g, by independence of the extra coordinate. We bound the number of image points by projecting to k coordinates, with k=d+1 in (a) and k=d+1−d′ in (b).
In (b), if Y is a basis of F^⊥, its rows Y_J are invertible and its restriction to I is in the column span of B, so B_J has rank d′. The integral kernel of B_J is saturated; extend a basis of it to a unimodular basis of Z^d with the kernel columns last. Trimming is basis-invariant; use the resulting B=(B_1,B_2) to define Φ, with (B_2)_J=0 and (B_1)_J square invertible. The transpose of Φ maps a normal (a,t) to (Ba,t). This injective map covers the real normal space of F by the restriction hypothesis, so Φ(F) has affine dimension k and normal lattice of rank d′. Split a basis matrix V of the image normal lattice into its first d′ rows V_1 and its remaining k rows V_2. At J the pullbacks give (B_1)_J V_1=Y_J C with C integral nonsingular, so |det(B_1)_J|·|det V_1|≥h(F^⊥).
Projection drops the first d′ coordinates. It is injective on differences in ker Vᵀ by invertibility of V_1. The projected integral differences lie in the kernel of x↦V_2ᵀx mod V_1ᵀZ^{d′}, a subgroup of index δ=|det V_1| since VᵀZ^{d+1}=Z^{d′}. In (a) use the identity projection, δ=q, B_2=B, J=∅ and an empty first minor of determinant 1.
Thus the projected image has affine dimension k in an index-δ coset. Its convex hull contains a simplex of volume ≥δ/k! by the integral determinant in a coset lattice basis. The lattice point bound in that basis yields count ≤k!·vol/δ+k≤(k+1)!·vol/δ, where vol is the hull volume. The hull lies inside the product of the projected trimming ellipsoid and the extra interval of length ≤g. The projection onto the B_2 coordinates has volume vol(Ball_{k−1})(g R_tr/√12)^{k−1}√det(B_2ᵀB_2), by taking the singular values of the projected ellipsoid map. Here Ball_j is the Euclidean unit ball of dimension j. By Cauchy–Binet and (B_2)_J=0, multiplying the square root by |det(B_1)_J| gives at most √C(N,k−1) h(Θ), since each corresponding block minor of B has magnitude ≤h(Θ); C denotes the binomial coefficient.
Writing j=k−1, the mass bound is therefore Pr[F]·δ·|det(B_1)_J|≤m(Θ)h(Θ)g^j (j+2)! vol(Ball_j)R_tr^j √[N^j/(12^j j!)]. For j=1,2,3 the constants multiplying R_tr^j N^{j/2} are 2√3, √2π, and 20π/(9√2), respectively, all within Λ_j by (I3). Substituting the index in (a) or the height inequality in (b) proves both bounds.

Regularization. For a saturated rank-d lattice on ≤N indices, d∈{1,2,3}, and m(Θ)≥μ+(3−d)ε, we will find a regular saturated superlattice of rank at most three losing at most (3−d)ε in density.
Induct downward on d. The dense rank-three bound includes regularity, proving d=3. For d≤2 take the prefix lattices Θ_k from the largest minor J of Θ, with densities m_k, heights h_k and height ratios s_k. Since m_k is nonincreasing, every m_k≥μ+(3−d)ε.
In increasing prefix order choose a largest fiber F_k, trimming by the preceding regular superlattice whenever that was constructed. Thus Pr[F_k]≥m_k−ε. Its saturated normal lattice contains Θ_k. If the containment is strict, its rank e exceeds d and is at most three by Pr[F_k]>g^{-4} and the rank fiber bound. Its density is at least μ+(2−d)ε≥μ+(3−e)ε. Use induction to choose a regular superlattice R_k of that normal lattice with density ≥m_k−ε−(3−e)ε≥m_k−(3−d)ε. If this occurs at the final prefix, R_k proves the claim.
Otherwise let j be the last prefix with a constructed R_j, or d−1 if none. For k≥j+1 before the final prefix, s_k≥g would make the new coordinate constant on the fiber and hence on F_{k+1}; its unit vector would be in F_{k+1}^⊥=Θ_{k+1} while vanishing on J, impossible. So the prefix bound makes m_k(m_kh_k)^{b−1} nonincreasing from k=j+1. It suffices to bound it there by μ(Γ_d/g^d)^{b−1}, because final density is ≥μ. When j=d−1 its value there is g^{-db}; the needed inequality is Γ_d^{b−1}≥g^{-d}/μ.
Otherwise put e=rank R_j. Apply the sparse transition bound with R_j, the next coordinate, and F_{j+1}. The normal lattice of F_{j+1} is Θ_{j+1} of rank d<e, largest minor at J in the old prefix, and its restrictions belong to the span of Θ_j and thus of R_j. Also F_{j+1} was trimmed by R_j. Therefore Pr[F_{j+1}] h_{j+1}≤Λ_{e−d}Γ_e/g^d by regularity. Since m_{j+1}≥μ, (I4) gives m_{j+1}≤A_inv Pr[F_{j+1}]. Meanwhile m_{j+1}≤m_j≤Pr[F_j]+ε≤g^{−d−1}+ε≤μP_d^{b−1} by (I4), using the strict normal rank increase at j. Multiplying these two estimates gives m_{j+1}(m_{j+1}h_{j+1})^{b−1}≤μ(A_inv Λ_{e−d}Γ_e P_d/g^d)^{b−1}≤μ(Γ_d/g^d)^{b−1} by (I4). Thus Θ itself is regular in this case.

Support induction and short representative.
Relabel the positive coordinates so the nonzero ones of v come first, say j=1,…,m. The scalar vᵀr only uses independent uniform coordinates. The largest atom cannot increase on adding an independent summand, by conditioning on that summand; moreover each nonzero coefficient gives an atom bound 1/g. Thus each nonempty prefix of the support has largest atom in (θ,1/g].
Inductively maintain a saturated regular lattice Θ on the first i coordinates, of rank d∈{1,2,3}, with v_{[i]} in its reduction and m(Θ)≥gp(v_{[i]}ᵀ)−3ε>μ. The first lattice is Z, with height 1 and density 1/g; Γ_1≥1 by (I4) and μ<1/g. At every step h=h(Θ)≤H_d, by regularity for d≤2 and the dense rank-three height bound for d=3.
To extend, project Θ onto a largest minor J. This is an isomorphism onto a lattice of determinant h, and each lifted infinity norm is bounded by the projected ℓ₁ norm. The ℓ₁ unit ball has volume 2^d/d!, so Minkowski’s second theorem bounds the product of successive minima by d!h. Mahler’s bound gives a basis with ℓ₁ lengths ≤λ₁, λ₂ and (3/2)λ₃, for the respective successive minima that are present. Hence the lifted basis B has product of column infinity norms ≤a_d h with (a_1,a_2,a_3)=(1,2,9). Write v_{[i]}≡Bc′ and set c=(c′,v_{i+1}), Φ(r)=(Bᵀr_{[i]},r_{i+1}). Trim a largest modular fiber cᵀΦ(r)=t by Θ to obtain F with density at least gp(v_{[i+1]}ᵀ)−ε>μ. Its image lies in a coset of index q because v_{i+1}≠0. If the image had full affine dimension d+1, the sparse bound and regularity would give density ≤Λ_d g^d h m(Θ)/q≤Λ_d Γ_d/q<μ by (I5).
Take the matrix of differences of the image points, of rank k≤d. The length of the trimming ellipsoid along coordinate j in the sense of maximum minus minimum is 2R_tr√[(Σ_Θ)_{jj}] by Cauchy–Schwarz in the ellipsoid metric. This is at most T_tr‖B_j‖_∞ by its covariance formula, with B_j the j-th column. The last coordinate differences are bounded by g−1≤T_tr. The determinant expansion bounds every k-minor by d!T_tr^d ∏_j‖B_j‖_∞, since the norms and T_tr are at least one. This is at most d!a_d H_d T_tr^d<q by (I5). The small-minor lift above yields an integral relation u on those differences reducing to c. Then (Bu_{[d]},u_{d+1}) is constant as a linear form on F, so its residue v_{[i+1]} lies in the reduction of F^⊥. The rank of F^⊥ is positive because that residue is nonzero, and at most three because Pr[F]>μ>g^{-4} and a rank-e lattice fiber has density at most g^{-e}. Also m(F^⊥)≥Pr[F]>θ−ε≥μ+2ε. Regularization supplies a saturated regular superlattice losing at most 2ε, proving the invariant.
For the last lattice, choose a largest minor at J and z_0 with Bz_0≡v_{[m]}. The coefficient lattice of z with z mod q in the line of z_0 has index q^{d−1}; z_0 mod q is nonzero since v_{[m]} is nonzero. Mapping by B_J gives determinant hq^{d−1}. By (I6) and integrality of h, d!hq^{d−1}≤β^d. The closed ℓ₁ ball of radius β has volume (2β)^d/d!, so shrinking it to the volume threshold if needed and applying Minkowski gives a nonzero lattice point B_Jz therein. The coordinate bound at J gives 0<‖Bz‖_∞≤β<q, so Bz reduces to a nonzero multiple of v_{[m]}. Extend by zeros and undo the relabeling, giving x_0=0.

add.label: Direct view
add.name: View
add.statement: For a target-group expression D and χ∈F_q, if val(D)=χκ identically at r, the sector stacks are symmetric, pass and satisfy the ties, and each W_c r=u_c; the plain key corner is χ. At such an identity, the coefficient D_{ab} for a second-group coordinate b=(H_{j,1}^{leg})^s vanishes unless a is a first-group F_{i,1}^{k_1}. The distinct monomials s_X υ^{k_c} y_i determine the cell and row. At such an identity, changing r to r′ changes the sector-s contribution by α_s Σ_c γ_c yᵀW_c(r′−r). Thus an identity with zero stacks holds formally and has χ=0. A formal identity forces χ=0; formally equal expressions have equal stacks. If D is not χκ identically at r, its probability of equaling χκ over uniform valid coins is ≤d_f/(q−D)≤ε_f. For two non-formally-equal source-group expressions, the analogous equality probability is ≤ε_f at every r.
add.proof:
On the valid coin grid the denominator-cleared equality is polynomial of degree ≤d_f by the degree premise, and its denominator is nonzero there. Each grid factor has size ≥q−D>d_f, so Schwartz–Zippel proves the probability claim and allows polynomial coefficient comparison in the identity case.
Put a=Ω_{12} and b=Ω_{22}. The first-group F exponents are π_{k_1}y_i and π_{k_1}(a y_i+b A_i). For each leg and j the only second-group poles in b are the two H coordinates, with numerators at the pole −a s_leg(B_j−y_j) and s_leg(B_j−y_j), times α_s. Multiply by b and set b=0 after clearing the other nonzero denominators; these other denominators are independent of a,b and can be canceled from the resulting polynomial identity. The constant first-group residues (all elements except F_{i,2}^{k_1}) are 1, ζτ^k, ζ′τ^k, ζ″y_i and π_{k_1}y_i, and the remaining residues are aπ_{k_1}y_i. Let p stand for a constant residue, indexed by its group element, and F for π_{k_1}y_i indexed by the coordinates F_{i,2}^{k_1}. The coefficients in a of degrees 2 and 1 in the pole identity are respectively
−Σ_{s,leg,j,F} α_s D_{F,H_1} F s_leg(B_j−y_j)
and Σ_{s,leg,j} α_s s_leg(B_j−y_j)(Σ_F D_{F,H_2}F−Σ_p D_{p,H_1}p),
where H_1,H_2 denote the respective coordinates in leg, sector and index j. Both vanish.
Replace y by B(τ)+x and take the coefficient of x_j. The factors after substitution at x=0 are independent for a fixed j: α distinguishes sectors, s_X υ^{k_leg} distinguishes legs without π_{k_1}, and 1, ζ, ζ′, ζ″ distinguish the remaining families without π. The powers of τ are independent and the B_i(τ) are independent since B(d_i)=e_i for i=0,…,N. For terms with π_{k_1}, extract ε-degree zero to get π s_X υ^{2k_1+k_leg}, distinct for cells of each kind, with B_i again independent. Hence the degree-two equation sets all F_{i,2} coefficients against H_1 to zero. The degree-one equation kills H_1 coefficients except F_{i,1}, and matches each of those with its F_{i,2},H_2 coefficient.
Next separate degree in α and the homogeneous class π in π,ζ,ζ′,ζ″ and Ω. The class-π pairs are the matched F,H coordinates, F_1 with search bases or G_2, and matching quotient, remainder and cancellation powers with bases. Summing the matched coordinates cancels Ω by matrix inversion. For sector s divide by α_s. Using the factor formula, the resulting equality is Σ_c γ_c b_c+Φ=χ_s κ, where χ_plain=χ and χ_α=−D_K, and
b_c=yᵀ(W_c r−u_c)+yᵀ(W_c−W_cᵀ)A(τ)+(P_{W_c}+h_c Z_c+Z_0 R_c)(τ).
The quotient h_c and allowed remainder R_c collect coefficients of the chunk powers. Each b_c is free of ε, υ and s_X.
